reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / GeneReviews mitochondrial disease
clinicalPearls: Typically presents in infancy or early childhood with psychomotor regression, hypotonia, feeding and swallowing difficulty, and often follows an intercurrent illness
The radiological signature is bilateral symmetrical T2 hyperintense lesions in the basal ganglia and brainstem, frequently with elevated lactate on MR spectroscopy
It is genetically heterogeneous: causative defects lie in either mitochondrial DNA (for example MT-ATP6, giving maternal inheritance) or numerous nuclear genes such as SURF1 (autosomal recessive)
The common final pathway is impaired oxidative phosphorylation, most often affecting complex I, complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) or pyruvate metabolism
Brainstem involvement can produce respiratory irregularity, abnormal eye movements, nystagmus and central apnoea
Blood and cerebrospinal fluid lactate are commonly raised, and the CSF-to-blood lactate ratio can be informative

Management is supportive with attention to nutrition, intercurrent illness and generic cofactor supplementation, avoiding respiratory-chain toxins and, where a pyruvate dehydrogenase defect is confirmed, considering a generically high-fat ketogenic dietary approach under specialist supervision
reference.pathophysiology: Leigh syndrome is a genetically diverse but phenotypically convergent disorder of mitochondrial energy metabolism. Whatever the underlying gene, the result is deficient ATP production, most often from defects of respiratory-chain complex I or IV, ATP synthase, or the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex. When the defect resides in mitochondrial DNA the disorder is maternally inherited and heteroplasmic with a threshold effect, whereas nuclear-encoded forms follow Mendelian, usually autosomal recessive, patterns. Chronically energy-starved neurons in the basal ganglia, thalamus, brainstem and cerebellum undergo the characteristic focal, bilaterally symmetrical necrosis with capillary proliferation, gliosis and demyelination that gives the disorder its descriptive name.
additionalDifferentials: Other mitochondrial encephalopathies including MELAS and MERRF
Biotinidase or biotin-thiamine-responsive basal ganglia disease
Wilson disease and other basal ganglia metabolic disorders
Kernicterus or hypoxic-ischaemic basal ganglia injury
Organic acidaemias such as glutaric aciduria
additionalInvestigations: Blood and cerebrospinal fluid lactate and pyruvate with calculation of the lactate/pyruvate ratio
Brain MRI with spectroscopy demonstrating symmetrical basal ganglia and brainstem lesions and a lactate peak
Plasma amino acids and urine organic acids to exclude mimicking metabolic disorders
Molecular genetic testing including mitochondrial DNA analysis and nuclear gene panels (e.g. SURF1)
Skeletal muscle biopsy for respiratory-chain enzyme assays where genetics are inconclusive
Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex enzyme activity when a PDH defect is suspected
redFlags: Brainstem dysfunction with central hypoventilation or apnoea
Rapid neurological regression triggered by intercurrent infection or fasting
Progressive bulbar weakness with aspiration risk
reference.prognosis: Leigh syndrome is generally progressive with a guarded outlook; classic infantile forms often follow a stepwise decline with intercurrent illnesses and reduced survival, though later-onset and some nuclear-gene forms can run a more indolent course.
pitfalls: Assuming a single gene: Leigh syndrome requires both mitochondrial DNA and nuclear testing because it is highly heterogeneous
Overlooking treatable phenocopies such as biotin-thiamine-responsive basal ganglia disease or a pyruvate dehydrogenase defect
Missing brainstem respiratory involvement that can cause sudden deterioration
Exposing patients to mitochondrial toxins or prolonged fasting that precipitate crises
